This month, we're sharing how we opened our bug bounty program to the public on HackerOne, and a look inside the graph-based architecture powering our multi-product booking engine. We're also highlighting recent media coverage on our AI practices, the engineering behind our One Checkout feature, and open roles across our global team. 🚀 On the Blog Agoda Launches Bug Bounty Program on HackerOne to Connect with Global Research Community We just opened our bug bounty program on HackerOne to the public, inviting the global security research community to help test Agoda's platform. Since 2016, we've run a private program with an invited group of ethical hackers, and this next step expands that collaboration to more researchers, more perspectives, and more opportunities to catch issues that internal teams and private programs might miss. In this post, we share why we made the move, what's in scope across Agoda.com, our APIs, and mobile application, and how the program is structured, including reward tiers, response targets, and submission guidelines for researchers who want to participate. 👉 Read the full blog → How Agoda's Multi-Product Booking Engine Powers Seamless Travel Bookings We recently shared how our Multi-Product Booking Engine (MPBE) brings hotels, flights, activities, and other travel products into a single, unified booking flow. In this post, we walk through the graph-based architecture and the asynchronous agent pattern that enable common steps, such as fraud checks, payments, and confirmation emails, to be reused across product types while still supporting product-specific workflows. The article also covers how we merge product-specific graphs into a single integrated workflow. 👉 Read the full blog 📰 Agoda in the News CIO ASEAN: Eleven Markets, One Vision — Agoda's CTO on the Future of Travel Tech in Southeast Asia In a video interview with CIO ASEAN, our CTO, Idan Zalzberg, discussed what it takes to build and scale digital technology across Asia-Pacific's eleven economies, with their fragmented payment systems, variable connectivity, and shifting regulatory frameworks. The conversation explores how Agoda treats that complexity as a problem worth solving rather than a constraint to work around. The interview also covers the AI question facing the travel industry; investing with discipline while guarding against disintermediation; engineering culture within a global conglomerate; the competition for senior tech talent across the region; and why data trust is becoming a genuine competitive differentiator. 👉 Watch the full interview → Frontier Enterprise: Agoda's AI Strategy: Fail Fast, Innovate Faster In an interview with Frontier Enterprise, our CTO, Idan Zalzberg, discussed Agoda's "inside-out" approach to AI: testing, refining, and validating new features internally before releasing them to customers. The article covers how the strategy is supported by Agoda's own infrastructure, with around 1 million CPU cores running across in-house data centers, and how our new APAC Tech Hub at One Bangkok now houses around 1,500 of our 2,000+ technology employees. The piece also explores Agoda's use of generative AI across the business, from Code Buddy, our AI code reviewer with a 92% satisfaction rate, to internal tools like Query Assist, our fraud detection work, and customer-facing features such as review summaries and the Property Ask Me Anything chatbot. 👉 Read the full article → CDOTrends: When AI Grades Its Own Coding Homework In a feature from CDOTrends, our CTO, Idan Zalzberg, walks through how Agoda manages AI-assisted coding at near-100% adoption, and how the team handles the new bottleneck this creates: code arriving faster than humans can review it. The piece describes how Agoda built an AI code reviewer that now handles more than half of all code changes, with a 92% developer satisfaction rate. The article also explores how the team manages variance in probabilistic systems, rerunning every reviewer change against hundreds of past evaluations, shipping model updates as blind experiments, and reviewing each change four times to reduce noise, alongside Zalzberg's "inside-out" philosophy of proving AI internally before rolling it out to customers. 👉 Read the full article → WiT: An Agoda Case Study: Combining Flights, Hotels, and Activities into a Single Transaction In a case study published by WebInTravel, our CTO, Idan Zalzberg, shared the engineering work behind One Checkout, Agoda's multi-product booking engine that lets travelers bundle hotels, flights, and activities into a single transaction, with one payment, one fraud check, and one confirmation flow. The feature went live on May 13 and is available on Agoda.com and the mobile app. The article also explores the architectural shifts that made it possible, including rebuilding workflows originally designed for single-product bookings, sequencing supplier confirmations across products with different cancellation terms and hold windows, and running the system across Agoda's four on-premise data centers. 👉 Read the full article → 🧑💼 Life at Agoda — Relocation Story From Indonesia to Bangkok: Ryan's Journey Ryan Owen Thionanda joined Agoda as a Staff Software Engineer after working as a Frontend Engineer at an Indonesian online marketplace, where he was based remotely in Medan during the COVID-19 lockdown. He chose to relocate to Bangkok to pursue a long-standing goal from his university days: working alongside diverse, international colleagues on large-scale problems. Today, he works on Agoda's data platforms, where his team is leaning into AI adoption. Outside of work, he enjoys exploring Bangkok's food scene, traveling around Thailand, and recreational running. He recently completed the Pattaya Marathon 2025 with his wife, who joined him in Bangkok after they got married. 👉 Read Ryan's full story → Join Our Global Team 🌍 We're hiring across a range of technical roles at Agoda, from software engineering and data science to product, infrastructure, and analytics. [_New research_](https://grow.cleverbridge.com/blog/sales-led-digital-buying-paths?utm_source=growthunhinged&utm_medium=paid-newsletter&utm_campaign=digitalswitch&utm_content=q2-2026)_ from Cleverbridge shows that while sales-led GTM isn’t going away, it is changing._

_Sales teams are focusing on upmarket, complex enterprise deals. Meanwhile, they’re offloading small deals, renewals, mid-cycle add-ons, and transactional upsells to self-serve tools. The result: more time actually selling, less time on busywork. And much healthier unit economics._

_Cleverbridge just released __[**part two of a new content series**](https://grow.cleverbridge.com/blog/sales-led-digital-buying-paths?utm_source=growthunhinged&utm_medium=paid-newsletter&utm_campaign=digitalswitch&utm_content=q2-2026)__** **__on this shift. It explores the cost-to-serve problem inside sales-led companies and how sales, CS, and digital buying paths work together._

Read the article here (https://grow.cleverbridge.com/blog/sales-led-digital-buying-paths?utm_source=growthunhinged&utm_medium=paid-newsletter&utm_campaign=digitalswitch&utm_content=q2-2026)


----------Here's the thing I keep coming back to after looking at the data: the companies most associated with replacing GTM jobs are the ones hiring most aggressively into those same roles.

Cursor is hiring SDRs. So is Decagon. So is OpenAI. While the broader market pulled back on SDR hiring by 21% year-on-year, AI-native startups more than doubled their SDR headcount. The companies selling the automation apparently aren't buying all of it.

That's the biggest surprise in the inaugural H1 2026 State of GTM Hiring report, built on real-time job post data from Sumble across US-based B2B digital native companies. The headline number isn't pretty — overall GTM job posts are down 15%, a trend that continued through April. But if you're trying to make sense of where GTM is actually headed, the story underneath that number is considerably more interesting.

Here’s a preview of my favorite takeaways:

* **SDR job posts are down 21%** – but the companies supposedly killing the SDR job have doubled their SDR headcount.

* **AI-natives are automating customer support** with 67% smaller teams. They are still investing in customer success.

* **Overall GTM job posts are down 15%**, even as AI companies raised $200B+ last year. More fundraising isn't translating into more jobs.

* **3-in-5 open GTM roles are AEs or solution engineers. **Buyers still want to talk to a human.

* **Growth marketing is the only marketing role that's actually up year-on-year.**

* **GTM engineering headcount has doubled.** It’s coming into its own with 400+ GTM engineers at US digital natives.

* **Clay pioneered GTM engineering; Claude Code is becoming the go-to tool.**

* **Marketers are more Claude-pilled than every GTM function** outside of GTM engineering.

----------
**Methodology note:**

This analysis is based on data from [Sumble](https://sumble.com/), which captures real-time job post data across 3 million verified companies. It focused on job posts in the US at B2B digital native and AI-native companies. Companies with a significant B2C motion were excluded.

Sumble uses job titles to auto-categorize job posts into top-level categories (Sales, Marketing, etc.) along with more specialized sub-categories (Growth Marketing, Product Marketing, GTM Engineering, etc.). Job post data can be noisy – one job post might have multiple open roles behind it or vice versa – and so the analysis was cross-checked against headcount data as well.

## SDR job posts are down 21% – but the companies supposedly killing the SDR job have doubled their SDR headcount.

SDR/BDR jobs have not been spared as more companies are turning to [automated and signal-based](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/the-best-ai-native-gtm-plays-you-re-not-running) outbound workflows. New job posts are down 21% year-on-year, below the rest of the hiring market.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/ae38308c-24aa-4265-ad89-914b0c5451a7/image.png?t=1779110128)
Caption: 

Here’s the surprise (and narrative violation). AI-native companies are aggressively adding SDR headcount while the rest of the market is pulling back. 

**SDR headcount at AI-native companies has more than doubled year-on-year.** It’s now the second fastest growing GTM role by headcount within AI-native companies. This trend is continuing today: AI-native companies are hiring 50% more SDRs as a share of their GTM job posts compared to all digital natives.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/78435457-43ce-4483-847f-aa94721aee29/image.png?t=1779229475)
Caption: 

Recent examples include Legora, Cursor, LangChain, Fireworks AI, Decagon, and even OpenAI. Anecdotally, many tech companies hire SDRs as a training ground for junior employees; top-performers quickly get promoted to AE. If you’re building an AI company, this is your permission to keep hiring SDRs.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/f92682b4-7619-4874-b8cd-265b50f20b9c/image.png?t=1779110164)
Caption: OpenAI is one of many AI-natives hiring SDRs to sell AI

## AI-natives are automating customer support with 67% smaller teams. They are still investing in customer success.

AI-natives aren’t automating SDRs. They are, however, automating customer support. 

Customer support represents only 2.2% of GTM headcount at AI-native companies, which is **67% smaller than other B2B digital natives** (6.6% of GTM headcount). This is especially striking because customer success headcount is comparable between the two.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/7e97c7dc-c39d-413a-ae78-7ba49fadfd16/image.png?t=1779219844)
Caption: 

In the job post data, **customer support saw the biggest year-over-year decline** **of every GTM role **(down 37%). This speaks to the growing traction of AI customer support products like Sierra ($15.8B valuation), Fin (formerly Intercom), Decagon ($4.5B valuation), Parloa ($3B valuation), Crescendo, and others.

———————————————————————————

## Overall GTM job posts are down 15%, even as AI companies raised $200B+ last year. More fundraising isn't translating into more jobs.

There were 22,988 GTM job posts in Q1 2026 for roles at US digital native companies. This is down 15% compared to Q1 2025, and the trend continued in April amidst the [sell-off](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/the-saas-empire-strikes-back) of SaaS stocks. These figures include sales, marketing, solutions, customer service, and business development jobs.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/2355d146-3d22-4f47-9028-ee24ce6ac117/image.png?t=1779110238)
Caption: 

AI-native companies did accelerate GTM hiring by nearly 50% year-on-year. That said, the overall volume is low: these are still only 5% of all digital native GTM job posts and 2% of GTM headcount.

I expected this to be higher given the fundraising headlines. AI companies raised over $200B last year according to Crunchbase and [venture funding](https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/funding-data-third-largest-year-2025/) was up 30% in 2025. More fundraising isn’t translating into more hiring.

———————————————————————————

## 3-in-5 open GTM roles are AEs or solution engineers. Buyers still want to talk to a human.

Sales is by far the largest category of GTM hiring. The typical GTM hiring ratio is 10 in sales for every 4 in solutions (SE), 4 in marketing, 3 in customer service, and 2 in RevOps. For analysis purposes, forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) have been bucketed into solutions.

Sales and solution engineer job posts are both fairly resilient. These jobs seem to be at a lower risk of being [replaced by AI tools](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/2026-claude-code-gtm-report) like Claude as buyers still want to talk to a real person.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/0bccb4a7-5840-47c7-856a-f25e34c3d624/image.png?t=1779110288)
Caption: 

These ratios are reflected in overall GTM headcount data as well. The Sumble dataset shows that >400,000 people are employed in GTM roles at US digital native companies with sales accounting for 40% of all GTM headcount.

———————————————————————————

## Growth marketing is the only marketing role that's actually up year-on-year.

Marketing job posts are down 20% year-on-year, and marketing now represents 15% of all GTM job posts within US digital native companies.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/d1d6d306-70bb-4578-9aae-3c1d61c80f5e/image.png?t=1779220242)
Caption: 

Marketing teams need to balance what Emily Kramer [calls](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sSuoV_YSrlw) fuel activities (messaging, content, design) and engine activities (channels, tools, analytics). The pendulum is certainly swinging from fuel to engine. Perhaps it’s overcorrecting?

Growth marketing is the only marketing role that’s up – **growth marketing job posts increased by 8% year-over-year. **Meanwhile, marketing operations is down 13%, product marketing is down 17%, and events marketing is down 23%.

———————————————————————————

## GTM engineering headcount has doubled. It’s coming into its own with 400+ GTM engineers at US digital natives.

There is one GTM role that’s clearly, unambiguously growing. That’s the GTM engineer.

There are now more than 400 GTM engineers at US digital native companies, and GTM engineering headcount has doubled year-on-year. Titles vary quite a bit for this role and might be called Growth Ops, AI Ops, RevOps Engineers, Lead to Opportunity Systems Engineers, or even the vague Member of Revenue Staff.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/c68daf99-2625-4680-81aa-30bcdda85658/image.png?t=1779220719)
Caption: 

To put this in perspective, there’s now one GTM engineer for every seven people in RevOps among AI-native companies. Across all digital native companies, the ratio is one GTM engineer for every 50 people in RevOps. The rise of GTM engineering has helped the total number of RevOps jobs remain stable even as all GTM hiring is down.

———————————————————————————

## Clay pioneered GTM engineering; Claude Code is becoming the go-to tool.

While Clay pioneered GTM engineering as a category, Claude Code is becoming a go-to GTM engineering tool as well. Claude was mentioned in 12% of Q1 2026 GTM engineering job posts, up 3x compared to Q4 2025.

**The risk sections conflate severity with likelihood without doing the work.** "Medium / Possible" appears on risks that have wildly different actual probability profiles. The Amazon competitive conflict is near-certain to manifest in some form. The Alibaba backdoor claim is speculative and adversarially motivated. Labeling both "Medium / Possible" is lazy calibration that a senior analyst would reject.

**The VCG competitive signals section is almost entirely descriptive.** "VCG has built superior media distribution relative to typical boutique consultancies" — compared to what baseline? Which boutique consultancies? What's the actual reach differential? This reads like an impression, not a finding. A Tegus analyst would have called three industry contacts and gotten actual numbers.

**The Anthropic emerging trends section buries the most important signal.** "Government-as-both-regulator-and-customer entanglement" is labeled a "strong signal" but gets the same paragraph length as the ESG carbon-removal item, which is a rounding error strategically. The weighting is wrong.

**The opportunities sections are generic.** "Early positioning in regulated science/pharma vertical" — this is true of every AI vendor entering life sciences. It's not an Anthropic-specific insight. It's a category observation dressed up as a finding. Cut it or make it specific: what does Anthropic have that Google and OpenAI don't in this vertical, and why does that matter right now?

**The timelines in both reports.** They read as chronologies, not as narratives with causation. The Anthropic timeline lists "Mythos model unsettles Washington policy" on May 8 and "Export ban on Fable 5/Mythos 5" on June 12 as separate entries without explicitly connecting them as cause and effect. ## The Ideas, Evaluated

**Pokémon Card / Persona Comparison**

This is the strongest engagement idea you've had. Here's why it works:

- It's not just a mirror, it's a *ranked mirror*. You're not just seeing yourself, you're seeing yourself *relative to someone real* at a specific stage.
- The stage-matching is the key insight. Not "you're like Elon Musk" — that's flattery. "You're showing traits consistent with Musk at the 2002 pre-SpaceX founding phase" — that's specific, citable, and creates a pull to either confirm or reject it.
- It works across personas because the underlying logic is the same: extract behavioral traits from your data, match against documented historical patterns of real people at real stages.
- The card format makes it shareable. That's a distribution mechanic built into the feature.

The risk: it becomes astrology if the trait matching isn't grounded in actual data. The card needs to show *why* — which three behaviors from your actual records map to which documented traits of that person at that stage. Without that, it's a personality quiz with a famous face on it.

**Audit — Thesis Format with Citations**

Clean upgrade. The PDF dump was never the right output. A structured report with cited sources at the end is exactly how you turn raw retrieval into something a professional can use, share, or act on. This is also the most buildable thing on this list right now because the retrieval infrastructure already exists — it's a formatting and structuring problem, not an architecture problem.

**Timeline — Expandable, Stage-Linked**

Good instinct to kill the "how many records in 2025" view. Nobody cares about storage counts. What people care about is *what was happening to me and where was I going.*

The expandable timeline linked to the Spotify/persona card is smart because it gives the card *depth*. The card says "you're at Musk 2002 stage" — the timeline shows the actual evidence trail that got you there. Tap the card, the timeline opens, you see the arc.

The future stage direction — "what do I need to do to get to the next stage" — is the most valuable part and also the hardest. That requires the system to have a model of what "next stage" looks like for your persona type. Doable, but it's a later layer.

**Source Feed — Artifacts and History**

Reframing source feed as a history of outputs rather than a list of connected accounts is the right move. Claude's artifact model is a good reference point. Every PDF generated, every action taken, every audit run — stored, retrievable, referenceable. This turns EYES from a session tool into a *record of your engagement with your own data over time.* That's meaningful.

## The Honest Build Reality

You asked: *can you do this now with the current build?*

Straight answer:

**Audit upgrade** — yes, closest to current capability. Restructuring output format doesn't require new infrastructure.

**Source feed as artifact history** — partially. The storage layer exists. The display layer needs work but it's not a new architecture problem.

**Timeline expandable view** — the data exists to populate it. The expandable UI and stage-linking is a frontend build, not a backend problem. Medium lift.

**Pokémon card / persona comparison** — this is the most complex. It needs:

2. A reference database of real people's documented traits at specific career stages — this is new data, not currently in the system

EYES — Technical & Strategic Brief (Founding Team Version)
Prepared by Abhi Godfred · April 24, 2026 · Rennes
0 · Why this document exists
This document is the full picture of EYES: architecture, security model, product, business model, and the current fundraising plan.
Context:  This was originally written as a highly technical, personalized brief for a specific technical reviewer. This version removes all personalization and rewrites the “you / your” framing so it can be used internally by the founding team as a shared reference.
Read time: 30–40 minutes. If you’re short on time, skim headings and go deep on Sections 4, 5, 6, and 7 (architecture, storage/legal design, security model, and the model strategy).
1 · The problem (mapped from enterprise Zero Trust to personal AI)
The core idea: the “data-flow problem” enterprises faced (and solved) is now hitting individuals — exactly when AI assistants are becoming the default interface to digital life.
The same Zero Trust principles — identity-aware access, consent granularity, auditability, and revocation — need to exist for the data flow between an individual and the AI applications they use.
2 · What EYES is (and what it isn't)
One-line:  EYES is the personal context and behavioral intelligence layer that any AI application can call — consented, EU-native, GDPR-compliant, identity-aware.
Two-sentence version:  Today every AI assistant ingests fragments of user data with no unified identity, no consent granularity, and no audit trail. EYES is the infrastructure layer that fixes this — like Plaid for personal context, with Zero Trust principles baked in from day one.
What EYES IS
A  data infrastructure layer  — OAuth ingestion, indexed storage, vector retrieval, three-tier separation by legal basis.
An  orchestration layer  — composes best-in-class models behind a unified API.
A  consent and audit framework  — every data access logged, every grant scoped and revocable, GDPR Article 15/17 first-class.
A  context API for AI applications  — eventually, an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that external AIs can call on behalf of a consenting user.
What EYES is NOT
Not a foundation model.
Not AGI.  The “thinking layer” framing is a long-term North Star, not an operating plan.
Not an agent.  The focus is the substrate that makes agents useful.
Not a recording device.  The core wedge is indexing years of existing digital history (backward) rather than only recording forward from purchase.
Not a chatbot wrapper.  The architecture is designed around personal data sovereignty from day one.
3 · Product surface
Three primary interfaces, in order of what ships first:
3.1 · Backward intelligence — search your past
User OAuth-connects platforms (Gmail, Reddit, Calendar, Notion, GitHub). EYES ingests history, embeds it, indexes it. User asks natural-language questions:
"What did I tell my investor about churn assumptions in Q3 2024?"
"Who introduced me to Sarah at the AWS event?"
"What was that restaurant in Tokyo I loved in 2019?"
"Have I ever flagged concerns about this vendor before?"
Returns a cited answer with source links — not a summary, evidence.
3.2 · Forward intelligence — proactive detection
Webhooks fire on incoming data. A detection pass extracts commitments, deadlines, renewal dates, people, decisions. System pushes notifications:
"Your AWS renewal is in 8 days. You flagged it as too expensive in February."
"Meeting with Sarah tomorrow. Last 5 interactions, last commitment, last open question."
"You haven't replied to your investor's last email — pattern suggests you should."
"Email volume to your co-founder dropped 70% over 3 weeks. Worth checking."
3.3 · Context API — EYES as substrate for other AI
MCP server interface. Users authorize external AIs (Claude/ChatGPT/Gemini/etc.) to query EYES on their behalf. Each session is scoped, time-bound, audited, and revocable.
4 · System architecture
Four trust boundaries, walked top to bottom.
